entries.title: Are flowers open at the same time every day?
entries.answer: If you watch the same clump of flowers twice in a day, you may see it open at one visit and closed at the other. Some kinds respond to changes in light and temperature, and some keep a daily rhythm of their own. A bright chicory head may be visible early in the day, while a flower visited by nighttime animals may open much later. A cloudy or unusually cool day can shift the times you see.
facts: To compare flowers fairly, check on the same plants more than once.

questions.text: Which blue roadside flower is often easier to see near morning?
Which kinds of visitors can reach flowers that open at night?
What can a visitor do while the flowers are open?

entries.title: Can a desert be cold?
entries.answer: A desert can be cold because what makes it a desert is the small amount of rain or snow it gets. Some deserts have very hot days, while others have winters well below freezing. In dry places, living things must get by with limited water. Some plants store water. Others grow and make seeds quickly when rain comes. The weather can change a lot across one desert, especially between high and low ground.
facts: A dry desert can have rocky hills, stony plains, or hard ground as well as sand.

questions.text: How does a saguaro cactus store water?
Where can desert rain briefly make a river?
How does wind build a dune?

entries.title: Can a rain forest be cool?
entries.answer: Some rain forests grow in places with cool or mild weather. In parts of the Pacific Northwest, moist ocean air brings heavy rain to the coast and mountains. Tall trees stand above thick moss, ferns, and fallen logs. Moss can even grow on the branches. A rain forest like this is called temperate because it grows outside the hot tropics. It can look much greener than nearby drier forests.
facts: The Hoh River valley in Washington state is home to a temperate rain forest.

questions.text: Why can a fallen trunk in a wet forest help new trees?
How is a tropical rain forest different?
Why does the Hoh Rain Forest get so much rain?

entries.title: Can an animal build places for other species to live?
entries.answer: When a beaver builds a dam, water can spread behind it and form a pond. The pond changes how fast the water flows and which ground stays wet. Some animals that live in still or shallow water can use the new space. Other animals may do better in a fast stretch of stream. A beaver is called an ecosystem engineer because its work physically changes the places where many other living things can live.
facts: A pond made by a beaver can change again if the dam breaks or is no longer cared for.

questions.text: How does a beaver build a dam and live nearby?
What kinds of plants can grow in a shallow pond?
What difference is there between a pool and a riffle?

entries.title: Can one lake have both warm and cold water?
entries.answer: In summer, sunlight can warm the top of a deep lake while the bottom stays much colder. The warmer water near the top usually floats above the colder water. In many lakes, the difference between the layers shrinks in cooler weather. Wind can then mix water from close to the surface with water from deeper down. This mixing, called lake turnover, can happen at different times and to different depths from lake to lake.
facts: Shallow ponds can mix much more often than lakes that are deep enough to keep separate warm and cool layers.

questions.text: Why is the edge of a pond a good place for plants?
How does sunlight change with depth in the ocean?
Why does ice float on water?

entries.title: Can prairie grass grow taller than a person?
entries.answer: In some Midwestern prairies, grasses such as big bluestem can grow taller than a person by the end of summer. Their roots spread deep into the soil, helping the plants find water and return the next year. Wildflowers grow between clumps of grass. Fire and grazing can change how much of the prairie is tall at one time, so some patches can look very different from others.
facts: There can be more living plant material below the ground of a prairie than above it.

questions.text: How do prairie plants come back after a fire?
Why are there wetlands in parts of the prairie?
Why do many temperate grasslands have few trees?

entries.title: Do some flowers get visitors at night?
entries.answer: When many bees have stopped flying for the day, some moths and bats are just starting to look for food. A flower that opens at night may have a scent its visitors can follow. It may also have pale petals that are easier to see in dim light. As a visitor drinks nectar or brushes past the flower, it can carry pollen away to another flower of the same kind.
facts: Bright lights can change the routes of some night-flying insects and keep them away from flowers they might visit.

questions.text: What happens when a visitor moves pollen to a new flower?
What is it like for some birds flying above bright lights at night?
How can a garden offer food to different insects through the year?

entries.title: How can a dry desert streambed suddenly fill with water?
entries.answer: A desert wash is a channel where water can flow after rain. It might lie dry for much of the year. If a storm pours water onto nearby hills faster than the ground takes it in, the runoff can rush into the channel. The rain may fall far away from the place where the water shows up. The flow can move rocks and sand before the channel dries again.
facts: A wash may still be dry while a storm upstream is already filling it with moving water farther away.

questions.text: Can deserts be cold as well as dry?
How can moving water change rocks and soil?
Why can a winding river leave behind a lake?

entries.title: How can a fallen log help the next forest grow?
entries.answer: In some damp forests, a tree seed lands on an old log instead of reaching the soil. As the wood breaks down, it can hold moisture and give the seed roots a place to grow. The trunk that helps the seedling is called a nurse log. If young trees grow along the length of it, their trunks can form a row long after the original log is gone.
facts: As an old log crumbles away, roots that grew around it can leave little gaps below the trees they hold up.

questions.text: How do fungi help break a fallen log down?
What makes a temperate rain forest so damp?
What happens while a dead tree is still standing?

entries.title: How can a forest grow in a swamp?
entries.answer: Some trees can grow in ground that stays wet for much of the year. Where those trees grow together in a wetland, the place may be a forested swamp. A swamp floor can include shallow pools, wet mud, and raised spots around roots or fallen trees. The mix changes with the water level. The plants that grow there are often different from plants in a nearby drier forest.
facts: Bald cypress trees can grow in warm swamps in the southeastern United States.

questions.text: How does a marsh differ from a forested swamp?
Why do river banks support different plants from dry ground?
How can a fallen log help young trees?

entries.title: How can one kind of animal change a whole shore?
entries.answer: On some rocky shores, sea stars eat mussels. If the sea stars disappear, mussels can take up more of the rock. That leaves less space where other animals or algae can live. A sea star can have a large effect even if it is only a small part of everything living there. Scientists call a species with an unusually large effect on its community a keystone species.
facts: The same animal can have a bigger effect in one habitat than it does in another.

questions.text: How does a sea star use its feet to pull on a mussel?
Why do California mussels grow in beds?
How can a sea otter change an underwater forest?

entries.title: How can you compare the way two kinds of leaves move?
entries.answer: Stand somewhere safe on a path and watch two kinds of tree while the breeze is blowing. One tree's leaves may flicker while the other tree's whole branch sways. Watch where each leaf joins the twig. Look for a long, thin stalk, a flat stalk, or a leaf that attaches directly. Keep track of more than one leaf on each tree. A single leaf could be still because it is tucked in a sheltered spot.
facts: You can record an observation by drawing what moved and where it moved.

questions.text: Why does a quaking aspen leaf move so readily?
What joins a leaf blade to the plant?
Which other details can help me compare leaves?

entries.title: How did glaciers leave thousands of little wet places?
entries.answer: Long ago, thick sheets of ice covered parts of what are now the northern United States and Canada. As the glaciers pulled back, they left many shallow dips across the land. Some dips collected water and formed little wetlands called prairie potholes. Some hold water for just part of the year. These pools are important places for ducks and other birds to raise their young.
facts: A prairie pothole can be surrounded by much drier grassland.

questions.text: How can a giant sheet of ice move?
What makes a seasonal forest pool different?
What grows in a tallgrass prairie?

entries.title: How do plants grow below a shady forest canopy?
entries.answer: Shrubs, young trees, and some small plants grow below the tallest trees. This part of the forest is the understory. Less light usually reaches it than the canopy above. Some plants can make enough food in dim light. Others grow faster in small sunny spots. In some forests with trees that lose their leaves, wildflowers can get plenty of light early in spring, before new leaves spread overhead.
facts: Low shrubs can give birds a place to nest under the tallest branches.

questions.text: Where do the highest leaves and branches meet?
What can happen in a new opening in the canopy?
Why do some forest trees drop their leaves each fall?

entries.title: How do prairie plants grow back after a fire?
entries.answer: In many tallgrass prairies, fires can burn dry stems without destroying every growing part of the grasses. Buds near or below the soil surface can survive and send up fresh shoots. Without fires, some shrubs and trees can spread into open grassland. The results depend on when the fire comes, how hot it gets, and which plants grow there. A prairie can have burned and unburned patches at the same time.
facts: Grazing animals may move toward a freshly burned patch to eat tender new growth.

questions.text: How can some tall grasses grow so high?
How does fire affect trees in a forest?
Why are grasses so common on some broad plains?

entries.title: How do savannas have trees and grass in the same place?
entries.answer: A tropical savanna has grasses with trees or shrubs scattered among them. Many savannas have a rainy season followed by a dry one. Grass may cover the ground in the wetter months and dry out later. Fire and grazing can help keep young trees from filling every open space. Some trees survive and grow above the grass, making spots of shade for animals in the heat.
facts: Savannas occur on several continents. They do not all have the same trees or animals.

questions.text: How is a temperate grassland different?
How do some prairie plants recover from fire?
What do lions do together in a group?

entries.title: How do trees live in the northern boreal forest?
entries.answer: Across much of northern North America and Eurasia lies a great stretch of forest called the boreal forest, or taiga. Winters are long and cold there. Many trees are evergreens with narrow needles instead of wide, flat leaves. Keeping needles can let a tree start making food when warmer weather returns. Some boreal trees, such as larches, have needles but drop them for the winter.
facts: Many boreal forests include spruce or fir trees, but the mix changes from one region to another.

questions.text: How do evergreen leaves handle winter?
What grows farther north where tall trees are scarce?
Why do some trees lose their leaves with the seasons?

entries.title: How does a barrier island shelter a coast?
entries.answer: A barrier island is a long, usually narrow island that runs near and roughly along a coast. Ocean waves hit its outer beach first. On the sheltered side, there may be a quiet bay, mudflats, or marshes. Wind and waves can move sand from one side of an island to the other. A big storm may open a new gap where water can flow between the bay and ocean.
facts: A row of barrier islands can be broken by narrow waterways called inlets.

questions.text: What lives in the mud on the sheltered side?
How can wind build a dune out of sand?
Why does a salt marsh flood when the tide comes in?

entries.title: How does a bend in a river become a lake?
entries.answer: As a winding river flows, it can wear away the outside banks of one bend. The two ends of that bend can slowly get closer. A flood or a change in the channel may let the river take a shorter route across the narrow strip of land. Mud and sand can close the ends of the old bend. What remains is a curved body of water called an oxbow lake.
facts: An oxbow lake may have the shape of a horseshoe or a wide letter U.

questions.text: Why does a river spread onto a floodplain?
Why is the ground near a stream often good for wildlife?
What might make a river carry more sand?

entries.title: How does a bog build up peat?
entries.answer: In many bogs, rain and snow supply most of the water. Peat moss and other plants grow on top of a thick layer of soaked plant remains called peat. Old plant pieces break down slowly because the wet soil has little oxygen. More pieces get added on top over time. The water in many bogs is acidic and low in nutrients, so the plants that do well there can be quite different from those in a nearby forest.
facts: Some mosses in a bog keep growing at their tips while older parts below them slowly become peat.

questions.text: How is a fen fed by a different source of water?
How can moss grow without true roots?
How can a pitcher plant catch an insect?

entries.title: How does sunlight get into a food chain?
entries.answer: Green plants use energy from sunlight to make sugars from water and a gas in the air called carbon dioxide. A plant uses those sugars to grow. When an animal eats part of the plant, it gets some of the energy stored in the food. A plant is a primary producer because it makes its own food. Many tiny algae do a similar job in ponds and oceans.
facts: Some food chains deep in the ocean begin with living things that use energy from chemicals instead of sunlight.

questions.text: How do plants make their own food?
How can life make food without sunlight in the deep ocean?
What do food chain arrows tell you?

entries.title: What can grow in Arctic tundra?
entries.answer: Arctic tundra has a long cold winter and only a short time each year when plants can grow. Mosses, grasses, and low shrubs can spread close to the ground. In many places, part of the ground below the surface stays frozen even in summer. Tall trees have trouble growing in these conditions. During the short summer, the top layer of ground can thaw and make room for roots and small pools.
facts: Being close to the ground can help keep some tundra plants out of strong winds.

questions.text: How can only the top of the ground thaw?
How can cold also limit trees on a high mountain?
What grows in the boreal forest south of some tundra?

entries.title: What can happen when an old field is left to grow?
entries.answer: Imagine a field that is no longer mowed. Tall grasses and small flowering plants may spread. Later, seedlings and shrubs can grow where their seeds land. Some may become trees that shade out the plants that first grew there. The change in the kinds of living things in a place over time is called ecological succession. Exactly what grows depends on the local weather, soil, seeds, and other changes in the land.
facts: A place that already has soil usually starts growing again differently from a bare surface of new rock.

questions.text: How can sunlight change a patch of forest after a tree falls?
What might lichens find on bare rocks?
How do seeds travel to a new patch of ground?

entries.title: What can you learn from comparing a seed parachute with a bur?
entries.answer: Imagine two plants ready to send their seeds away. A dandelion makes a light seed parachute of hairs that spread in the air. The air can lift a small fruit with a seed inside even if no animal walks by. A burdock has a heavier hooked bur. Its hooks can travel on fur, but need something to brush past and catch them. Look at a photo or fallen piece of each. Draw the shape that makes it good at reaching a new place, then explain what has to happen for it to move.
facts: One plant structure works with moving air, and the other works by gripping a surface.

questions.text: What is attached to the dandelion's white hairs?
What part makes a bur cling to a sock?
What other ways can seeds leave a parent plant?

entries.title: What do the arrows in a food chain show?
entries.answer: Imagine grass, a rabbit that eats the grass, and a fox that eats the rabbit. In a food chain, an arrow leads from grass to rabbit, and the next leads from rabbit to fox. Each arrow shows the direction in which food and energy pass. The chain follows just one possible route. A real rabbit might eat several plants, and it might be food for more than one animal.
facts: In most food chains, a plant or another living thing that makes its own food is near the start. That living thing is called a primary producer.

questions.text: How do many food chains fit together?
Why can most food chains begin with a plant or alga?
What happens to old leaves when nothing eats them right away?

entries.title: What grows in a freshwater marsh?
entries.answer: A freshwater marsh often has shallow water and plants with soft stems. Cattails and some grasses grow with their roots in wet ground while their leaves stick into the air. Ducks and other birds can feed in open patches or hide among the stems. In a swamp, woody trees or shrubs are usually the plants that stand out. Both kinds of wetland can have deeper and shallower spots.
facts: Some freshwater marshes fill and drain with river tides even though their water is mostly fresh.

questions.text: What kind of wetland can grow a forest of trees?
Why do cattails have fluffy brown heads?
How does a coastal salt marsh differ?

entries.title: What happens when a tall forest tree falls?
entries.answer: When a tall tree falls, it can leave a hole in the forest canopy between the branches of its neighbors. Sunlight reaches more of the ground below that hole. Plants already growing there may grow faster. Seeds that need bright light may sprout. As years pass, the branches of nearby trees or the tops of new trees can fill the space again. While that happens, the fallen trunk creates a different home near the forest floor.
facts: Many small gaps can give a forest patches with young and old trees growing side by side.

questions.text: What can grow on a fallen trunk?
What is the shady understory?
How can plants return to an old field?

entries.title: What is a forest canopy?
entries.answer: The highest branches and leaves of many trees together form a forest canopy. It is a kind of roof, with holes where light falls through. Leaves high up often get more sunlight than plants near the ground. Birds can nest on branches or feed on insects among the leaves. Wind can also reach that upper layer more strongly than it reaches the sheltered land below.
facts: A forest can have trees of several heights, so the canopy is rarely like a flat ceiling.

questions.text: How do plants grow in the shade under the canopy?
What changes when a tall tree falls and light gets through?
How do leaves turn sunlight into food?

entries.title: What is a tide pool?
entries.answer: When the sea goes out, water can stay behind in a hollow in the rocks. That little pocket of seawater is a tide pool. A pool may hold snails, anemones, and other animals even when the rocks around it look dry. These pockets form within the intertidal zone, the strip of shore that tides cover and uncover. Sunshine can warm the trapped water, and rain can make it less salty. The next high tide may wash over the whole pool and bring a fresh supply of seawater.
facts: A tide pool is only one kind of home on a rocky shore. Some shore animals live on exposed rock outside the pools.

questions.text: Why does the ocean rise and fall?
Where are the high and low zones on a rocky shore?
How does a sea anemone catch food?
How do mussels hold on when waves crash?

entries.title: What lives in a tidal mudflat?
entries.answer: At low tide, a wide stretch of soft mud may appear along a quiet coast. You might see holes, tiny trails, or birds poking their bills into the mud. Worms and some clams live below the surface, where the mud can stay damp until water covers it again. Wading birds can feed on those little animals. When the tide rises, some fish may come over the same flat to feed.
facts: Fine grains carried by water can settle where waves and currents are gentle.

questions.text: Why does the water come back to cover the mud?
What happens when river water mixes with seawater?
Where do horseshoe crabs lay eggs?

entries.title: What makes a fen different from a bog?
entries.answer: A fen is a wetland that often builds up peat, just as a bog can. Much of its water comes from groundwater or from a nearby slope. That water can carry minerals it picked up as it passed through soil and rock. The minerals can make conditions in a fen different from those in a rain-fed bog. Some fens have sedges, which look a bit like grass, growing among low shrubs.
facts: A fen can be harder to spot than a pond because its water may be hidden below plants.

questions.text: How can water travel through the ground?
How does peat build up in a bog?
Where can water from underground reach the surface?

entries.title: What makes a place a freshwater wetland?
entries.answer: A freshwater wetland has water in or above the soil for long enough to shape which plants and animals can live there. Some wetlands have puddles you can see. In others the ground is soaked below a leafy surface. The water may come from rain, a nearby river, or groundwater rising from below the surface. Wetlands can give wildlife room to feed, and some hold extra water when nearby rivers rise.
facts: Not every wetland stays underwater throughout the year.

questions.text: What makes a marsh different from a swamp?
How can a pool dry up and still be a home?
What happens when a river rises out of its banks?

entries.title: What makes an old-growth forest special?
entries.answer: An old-growth forest has had a long time to develop features that are often missing from younger forests. There may be very large old trees, smaller young ones, and trunks lying on the ground. Places where branches have opened up can let sunlight reach the ground. A single big tree does not tell you how old the whole forest is. Scientists look at several clues, and the features vary from region to region.
facts: Standing dead trunks and fallen logs can remain in some old-growth forests for many years.

questions.text: How is a fallen log used by young trees?
How can a patch of sun change a forest?
Who can live inside a standing dead tree?

entries.title: Where do the materials in fallen leaves go?
entries.answer: A tree drops a leaf into the leaf litter on the ground. Small animals can tear it into pieces. Fungi, bacteria, and other decomposers help break those pieces down. Some of the materials from the leaf enter the soil, where plant roots can take in some of them again. Other materials can leave as gases or move with water. Nutrients are materials living things use to grow, and some can be used over and over in an ecosystem.
facts: Leaves can break down faster in a warm, damp place than in a cold, dry one.

questions.text: What happens when fungi grow through fallen wood?
Why can an old log help a seed sprout?
How does a compost pile change food scraps?

entries.title: Where is the intertidal zone?
entries.answer: Stand back from a shore and imagine two lines across it. One marks how high the water reaches at high tide. The other shows how far it drops at low tide. The shore between those lines is the intertidal zone. Animals near the upper line spend more time exposed to air than those near the lower line. Which animals you find can change as you move down the rocks.
facts: An intertidal zone can be a sandy beach or a wide mudflat instead of a rocky slope.

questions.text: How can seawater stay behind when the tide goes out?
What lives in a tidal mudflat?
How does a barnacle stay on a rock?

entries.title: Who lives in a dead tree that is still standing?
entries.answer: A dead tree that has not fallen is called a forest snag. As some of its wood softens, a woodpecker may dig a hole to nest in. An old hole can later shelter a different bird or a small mammal. Tiny animals can hide in cracks or under loose bark. Standing dead trees eventually fall, changing from a high shelter into a log on the ground.
facts: A snag can be useful to wildlife even after it has lost most of its smaller branches.

questions.text: What might grow on the tree after it falls?
How do fungi break wood down?
Why do some old forests have trees of different ages?

entries.title: Who lives in the seaweed washed onto a beach?
entries.answer: Waves often leave strips of seaweed and other natural material along a beach. This pile, called beach wrack, is food and shelter for small animals such as beach hoppers. Beach hoppers are tiny relatives of crabs that can jump away as you walk near them. Birds can feed on small animals in the pile. Wrack can gather along the highest part of the beach reached by a recent tide.
facts: A beach can have more than one wrack line left by water that reached different heights.

questions.text: Why does the water reach different heights on a beach?
How can a sandy island shelter smaller habitats?
What can a shorebird find by probing in mud?

entries.title: Why are forest edges different from the middle of a forest?
entries.answer: Where woods meet a field, the trees are open to the sky on one side. There can be more sunlight and wind close to that edge than deeper among the trees. Dense shrubs can grow in the new light, and some birds prefer those shrubs. Other living things do better in the cool, sheltered forest interior. Cutting a big forest into small pieces usually makes more edge for the same amount of woodland.
facts: Some edges form naturally along rivers and open meadows.

questions.text: How can separate pieces of habitat change wildlife’s travels?
Why does a new hole between tall branches change what grows?
What lives in the shady understory?

entries.title: Why can a city stay warmer than places nearby?
entries.answer: On a sunny day, streets, roofs, and walls can warm up and hold some of that heat. At night they can release heat slowly, leaving some parts of a city warmer than greener places nearby. A neighborhood with many buildings and little shade can be hotter than a leafy part of the same city. Scientists call this pattern an urban heat island. Its size changes with the weather and the place.
facts: A grassy park and a parking lot only a short walk apart can feel different on the same afternoon.

questions.text: How can a street tree cool the space under its leaves?
Can a green roof hold some rain?
How can sunlight warm a surface without touching it?

entries.title: Why can a grassland have so few trees?
entries.answer: Grasses cover broad plains in places with a climate that can support them but often limits trees. The amount of rain is one part of the story. Fires, grazing animals, and dry seasons can also make it hard for trees to spread. Many grasses grow from buds low on the plant, where they can stay safe during grazing. Not all grasslands are alike, and trees may grow where water is easier to find.
facts: Temperate grasslands have several names around the world, including prairies and steppes.

questions.text: What grows in a tallgrass prairie?
How does a warmer savanna differ?
What helps grasses grow back after a fire?

entries.title: Why can a woodland wildflower do well before the trees have leaves?
entries.answer: The ground in a leafy forest can get a lot of sunlight in early spring. Most of the tall branches haven't made their new leaves yet. Some little woodland plants use that bright time to make leaves and flowers while there's enough light. When the tree leaves spread out overhead, the forest floor becomes shady. Some early flowers then lose the parts growing above the ground and keep living in roots or underground stems.
facts: A short-season flower like this may be called a spring ephemeral.

questions.text: What happens to a yellow trout lily later in the year?
Where does most of the light land once the tall tree leaves spread out?
How can a stem stay alive below the ground?

entries.title: Why do food chains make a web?
entries.answer: A food web shows several paths that food takes through a place. Think of a pond where young insects eat algae. Small fish might eat those insects or tiny animals that drift in the water. A heron might catch a fish or a frog. If you draw an arrow from every food to the animal that eats it, you get a web of connections instead of a single chain.
facts: A food web can help you ask what other animals might be affected when one food becomes scarce.

questions.text: Where does an arrow in a food chain point?
Why can a sea otter matter to a kelp forest?
How can one kind of animal change what others live nearby?

entries.title: Why do so many pond plants grow at the edge?
entries.answer: Near a pond’s edge, the water is often shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom. Some plants can put roots in the mud and send leaves up to the air. Others grow with floating leaves or stay completely under water. A thick group of plants offers insects and young fish places to hide. Out in deeper water, less light reaches the bottom, so a different set of living things may do well.
facts: Plants are not the only living things that use sunlight near the top of a pond. Tiny algae do too.

questions.text: Why can a deep lake have layers?
What makes a freshwater marsh different from a swamp?
How do plants use sunlight to make food?

entries.title: Why do some forest pools disappear in summer?
entries.answer: A low spot in a forest can collect rain and melted snow and turn into a shallow pool. In some years that same spot dries up by summer. A temporary pool like this is called a vernal pool. A pool that dries regularly often has no fish living in it all year. That can give some salamanders and frogs a place to lay eggs with fewer animals likely to eat them.
facts: A vernal pool can be too dry to find in summer even though it was busy with life in spring.

questions.text: How can a wetland stay hidden in dry-looking land?
Why do grown salamanders head back to a spring pool?
How does water move from the ground into the air?

entries.title: Why do trees stop growing high on some mountains?
entries.answer: As you go up a high mountain, there may be a place where you stop seeing tall trees. This is the alpine treeline. Above it, the air is often cold and windy, and summers can be too short for most trees to grow tall. Low plants may still grow in sheltered places or near the ground. The height of a treeline changes with local weather and the shape of the mountain.
facts: Some trees just below the treeline are short and bent instead of straight and tall.

questions.text: What grows in the cold Arctic tundra?
How can northern evergreens handle long winters?
How can a mass of snow turn into moving ice?

entries.title: Why does a deciduous forest change with the seasons?
entries.answer: Many forests in places with cold winters have broad-leaved trees such as maples and oaks. These trees usually lose their leaves in fall and grow new ones in spring. That can make the forest floor much brighter before new leaves spread overhead. In summer those leaves cast shade again. Some other kinds of trees can lose their leaves during a dry season instead of a cold one.
facts: A tree that regularly loses all its leaves in one season is called deciduous.

questions.text: Why do some leaves turn yellow or red before they fall?
How do some trees keep their leaves all year?
What grows in the shady part of the forest?

entries.title: Why does a stream look rough in some spots and smooth in others?
entries.answer: A shallow stretch of a stream can have rocks or gravel close to the surface. Water bumps over them and makes ripples. This kind of spot is called a stream riffle. In a nearby deeper pool, the water often moves more slowly and the top may look smooth. Both places give stream animals different options. Fish may rest in a pool, while small insects can hold onto rocks in the faster water.
facts: A stream can have many riffles and pools along just one short stretch.

questions.text: How does a young freshwater mussel move to a new part of a stream?

entries.title: Why does a tropical rain forest stay green?
entries.answer: Tropical rain forests grow where the weather is warm and wet through much of the year. Trees there generally do not all drop their leaves in the same season. A tree can grow some new leaves while older ones fall, so the top of the forest stays green. Under the highest branches it can be quite shady. Vines and plants that live on branches can reach a brighter spot without growing a giant trunk.
facts: The tallest trees in some tropical rain forests stick up above most of the other trees.

entries.title: Why would an ant carry away a seed it cannot eat?
entries.answer: Some seeds carry a little soft part on the outside that is rich in food. An ant can find that part and carry the seed away, sometimes to its nest. Once the ant has eaten the soft piece, the harder seed can be left behind. If there's enough water, warmth, and space where it lands, it may start growing there. The ant gets food and the plant gets a chance to reach new ground.
facts: Trilliums are one group of forest plants whose seeds can travel with ants.
